extracted.intended_audience: educated general public / readers of The Spectator (early 18th‑century polite society)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of social‑conduct and rhetorical guidelines embedded in Spectator essays and readers' letters: guidance on marital behaviour, manners, church and theatre etiquette, praise vs. flattery, translation fidelity, and methods of disputation. These are prescriptive norms and evaluative remarks meant for polite society and writers/translators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility, fidelity, and benevolence toward one's wife
rubrics_metrics.description: Husbands must not treat an helpless Creature with Unkindness, return Evil for Good, deceive a Woman with Appearances of Affection and Kindness for no other End but to torment her, or be false to their Word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: the essay condemns husbands who break promises or feign affection to gain power over their wives; such behaviour is presented as base and beneath Reason and Gentlemanly Character. Guidance stresses honouring promises, gratitude for trust, avoiding deception, and that unkindness from a husband makes both parties miserable. (Examples and rhetorical admonitions are provided in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected moroseness (don't adopt austerity to show independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some men, to appear free and untrammelled, adopt an austerity or affected moroseness—becoming tyrants at home so as 'to seem Masters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns this posed motive (avoiding being thought submissive) leads to bitterness, severity of look, and ultimately real contempt or alienation of affection. Advice: voluntary civility is generous and manly; affected hardness will become real and ruin domestic happiness. (Consequences and corrective persuasion are discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentlemanly civility is not weakness; practise voluntary benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be civil at least is not beneath the Character of a Gentleman; tender Affection towards one who would make it reciprocal betrays no Softness or Effeminacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends persuading men that voluntary civility and benevolence (not only obligations) are signs of greatness of soul. It cites a maxim (that a gentleman should make the inclinations of a woman of merit go along with her duty) and argues such behaviour improves marriage, family harmony, and public manners. (Offers both moral and practical benefits.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrain from audibly repeating the minister in church services
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people disturb others at Church by their Repetition of the Prayers after the Minister, and even repeat the Absolution and Commandments in a particularly audible manner—sometimes as loud as the minister himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is called 'extremely offensive' and irreligious inadvertency. The writer asks for mere mention of the offence (public censure) to effect amendment rather than ridicule. (No technical scoring—social corrective recommended.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not disrupt public entertainments by ostentatious behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members who make ostentatious displays—leaping over spikes, showing off in side‑boxes, vociferating, repeatedly appearing at doors or behind curtains—diminish the pleasure of the audience and are presumptuous and unwarrantable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific unwanted behaviours are enumerated (showboating, noisy vociferation, repeated stage appearances). The letter notes such conduct must be noticed and (later) rendered criminal by order ('no Person is to be admitted behind the Scenes'). Guidance: avoid such distractions; observe official injunctions. (Example provided from a particular performance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper salutation and public forms of address should not be mere affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: New fashions of bowing and saluting (taking a gross of the room by continual bows, resulting in kissing as a salutation) disrupt established country good breeding and leave people unsure whether such gestures (kissing as civility) are proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers ask for judgment on whether kissing is civility or salutation; implicit guidance is to evaluate new fashions critically and preserve sincere good breeding rather than imported affectations. (Social norm guidance; request for authoritative opinion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the love of flattery; prefer sincere, just praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Flattery is a pernicious disease of the mind: it awakens Self‑Love and corrupts judgment. The art of praising justly is laudable—praise that resembles a skilful painter retaining features while softening the picture into an agreeable likeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast flattery (insidious, leads to vanity and coxcombry) with genuine praise (encourages virtue and rewards merit). Examples: Germanicus secretly hearing sincere soldierly praise; Malvolio's envious praise is ironically the most trustworthy. Advice: cultivate the ability to praise justly and beware flattering motives. (Moral and psychological consequences discussed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses to praise and dispraise indicate character; cultivate a temper that can bear both
rubrics_metrics.description: A generous mind is most sensible of praise and dispraise; noble spirits are invigorated by due honour and depressed by neglect, but only the purest spirits are so affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay compares sensitivity to praise/dispraise to a thermometer: only the highest souls expand or contract. Implicit guidance: cultivate virtue and humility so one is strengthened by praise and not ruined by it. (Psychological observation serving moral counsel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reasoned questioning (Socratic method) where appropriate in debate
rubrics_metrics.description: Socratic method: ask question upon question until the adversary is convinced out of his own mouth that his opinions are wrong. This method drives an enemy into a corner, seizes passes for escape, and forces surrender by examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an effective method of argumentative conquest by subtlety and interrogation. It is contrasted with other methods; recommendation: use questioning to expose contradictions rather than blunt force. (Effectiveness and mode are described.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of endless scholastic syllogism and hair‑splitting (Aristotelian/academic dialectic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotelian/academic method invents a variety of small weapons called syllogisms and distinctions; prolonged scholastic wrangling can turn good sense into an infinite subdivision of objections and answers, producing interminable dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticises university syllogistic debate for cutting good sense into an infinity of distinctions. Implicit advice: avoid overreliance on technical syllogisms that obscure judgment; favour clarity over subtle pedantry. (Historical examples and critique provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use force, torture, or bribery as legitimate means of convincing others
rubrics_metrics.description: The author enumerates methods used historically—Argumentum Bacilinum (club‑law), arguing by torture (rack, faggots), convincing by ready money (bribery)—and shows they convert by coercion or corruption rather than reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are criticised as immoral or degrading even when effective: using physical violence, execution, torture, or monetary inducements to win assent is condemned. The passages offer historical examples (universities, state force, inquisitions) as warnings; implicit prescriptive norm is to reject coercive or corrupt means in favour of rational persuasion. (Moral censure and historical illustration.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize other non‑rational modes of 'argument' (arguing by poll or wager) and their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing by poll (appealing to numbers) or by wagers (placing stakes) are methods of managing controversy that substitute other forces for rational proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned among methods of debate: they may 'succeed' but are not genuine reasoning. Implicit guidance: be wary of equating popularity or betting with truth; these are persuasive tactics, not proofs. (Examples given; cautionary note.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's fidelity principle: keep close to the original meaning while making English fit
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator (writer of a submitted translation) says he kept 'as near the Meaning of the Greek as I could, and have only added a few Words to make the Sentences in English fit together a little better than they would otherwise have done.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as recommended practice for translation: preserve the original author's meaning and style as much as possible, only adding minimal words for English idiom. (Explicit example and corrective comparison with earlier looser translations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing a spouse: beware marrying for wealth hoping to reform a partner
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent laments leaving public admiration to marry for wealth into the arms of a fool, expecting superior understanding to make him tractable; instead, he found cunning and suspicion and that attempts at cheerfulness were viewed as insurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit advice: choose partners for compatible disposition and sense rather than wealth alone; do not assume you can easily reform a spouse. (Personal anecdote as cautionary example.)
